rats adjust the total amount of running they do to the total amount of drinking they are allowed to do.
rats adjust schedule performance to minimize deviations from baseline response rates.
rats under nondeprived schedules will run more and drink less when running is contingent on drinking, compared with when it is not.

the data presented here do not support a molar regulation model of the type proposed by Staddon and Higa.
the molar equilibrium hypothesis is not supported by the present data.

the effects of schedule contingencies depend on their interaction with the behavioral and motivational properties of the organism.

molar regulation does not occur under all conditions and that the conditions for its occurrence have not yet been identified.

behavior is a system, and that the system-specific nature of behavior needs to be taken into account when developing models of behavior.
